speakers.name: Dr. Rajendra Prasad
speakers.positionSummary: Controls admissibility, sequencing and the transition from amendments to general debate.

speakers.name: M. R. Jayakar
speakers.positionSummary: Moves to defer further consideration so absent parties can participate and the Assembly's work is not frustrated.

speakers.name: B. Pattabhi Sitaramayya
speakers.positionSummary: Intervenes repeatedly on the procedural character and priority of Jayakar's proposal.

speakers.name: Mohan Lal Saksena
speakers.positionSummary: Raises the rule that an amendment should be formally moved before the mover develops the speech.

speakers.name: K. Santhanam
speakers.positionSummary: Challenges the internal logic of Jayakar's legal argument about what the preliminary meeting can do.

speakers.name: N. V. Gadgil
speakers.positionSummary: Rejects the claim that the Cabinet Mission text prohibits consideration at this stage.

speakers.name: R. K. Sidhwa
speakers.positionSummary: Contests Jayakar's reliance on the absence of the States as a reason to defer the Resolution.

speakers.name: Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel
speakers.positionSummary: Rejects additional interpretations or concessions beyond the 16 May statement and later joins the adjournment exchange.
speakers.stance: Assembly should proceed on accepted basis

speakers.name: Suresh Chandra Banerjee
speakers.positionSummary: Presses the practical question of how long the Assembly should wait if the Muslim League does not join.

speakers.name: Govind Ballabh Pant
speakers.positionSummary: Challenges Jayakar's interpretation of the States' position and the claim that their participation depends on the Muslim League.

speakers.name: Hari Singh Gour
speakers.positionSummary: Attempts to amend Jayakar's amendment with a much wider proposal on communal representation; the Chair rules it out of order.

speakers.name: Diwan Chaman Lall
speakers.positionSummary: Argues that Jayakar's amendment is substantive, not merely procedural.

speakers.name: Somnath Lahiri
speakers.positionSummary: Defends a broader amendment as action flowing from the Resolution's aims; the Chair rules it out but promises speaking time later.

speakers.name: Unnamed Member
speakers.positionSummary: Briefly interjects during Lahiri's procedural argument.

speakers.name: Syamanandan Sahaya
speakers.positionSummary: Moves textual changes aimed at making the Resolution workable while avoiding formulations he thinks could deter the States.

speakers.name: N. G. Ranga
speakers.positionSummary: Questions whether a member should make repeated speeches while moving several amendments.

speakers.name: Uday Chand Mahtab
speakers.positionSummary: Declines to move his listed amendment.

speakers.name: Shri Krishna Sinha
speakers.positionSummary: Supports the original Resolution, emphasising popular sovereignty, a democratic decentralised republic and minority safeguards.

speakers.name: Several Members
speakers.positionSummary: Respond collectively when the Chair asks how long the House should continue sitting.

interventions.summary: The Chair resumes discussion of the Objectives Resolution and calls M. R. Jayakar to move his amendment.
Jayakar introduces his case: the Assembly should avoid a course that could make its constitution-making work ineffective and should consider the legal limits of this preliminary stage.
Pattabhi points out that the proposed amendment is, in substance, asking the House not to continue consideration now.
Saksena asks that Jayakar formally move the amendment before continuing his speech.
Jayakar formally proposes delaying further consideration so the Muslim League and Indian States can participate if they choose.
Santhanam argues that Jayakar's own opening clause faces the same objection Jayakar raises against Nehru's Resolution; the Chair tests the procedural implications with the House.
The Chair treats both the Resolution and Jayakar's amendment as in order and directs the debate to continue on the merits rather than reopen the threshold legal point.
Gadgil rejects the claim that the relevant Cabinet Mission clause contains a prohibition on proceeding.
Sidhwa disputes the argument that the present absence of State representatives is itself a valid reason for delay; the Chair classifies it as argument, not a point of order.
Patel challenges Jayakar's use of later British interpretations or concessions beyond the agreed Cabinet Mission statement.
Banerjee asks the practical question: if the Muslim League stays away, how long should the Assembly wait? The Chair asks him to reserve the argument for his turn.
Pant disputes Jayakar's interpretation of the princely States' likely conduct and objects to speaking for them without their representatives.
Jayakar closes by warning that proceeding now could deepen division and frustrate the Assembly's work; his core recommendation remains temporary deferment for wider participation.
Hari Singh Gour argues that if Jayakar's amendment is admissible, his own further amendment should also be considered; he frames his proposal as a correction to Jayakar's text.
The Chair rules Gour's proposed text out of order and sets a sequence for considering other amendments together with the main Resolution.
Pattabhi argues that Jayakar's proposal should receive priority because it effectively seeks adjournment of the Resolution's consideration.
Chaman Lall counters that Jayakar's proposal is itself substantive because it alters the constitutional proposition as well as seeking delay.
Lahiri argues that an amendment may propose action that advances the original Resolution's aims and therefore need not be confined to narrow textual correction.
An unnamed member briefly questions whether the precedent Lahiri invokes is formally reported.
The Chair rules Lahiri's amendment out of order but states that Lahiri will be given an opportunity to speak on the main Resolution later.
Sahaya proposes changes to the opening paragraphs so that the Assembly moves toward an independent sovereign republic while wording the route and territorial stages more explicitly.
Ranga questions whether multiple amendments should permit repeated speeches by the same member.
Sahaya narrows another clause to avoid a formulation he believes could alienate the princely States while preserving popular sovereignty as the core principle.
interventions.excerpt: all power and authority are derived from the people

interventions.summary: Uday Chand Mahtab declines to move his amendment.

After confirming that the remaining listed amendments have been withdrawn or disposed of, the Chair opens the Resolution and surviving amendments for general discussion and asks speakers to be concise.
Shri Krishna Sinha supports Nehru's original Resolution and presents popular sovereignty, democratic decentralisation and minority safeguards as its central constitutional features.
interventions.excerpt: ultimate sovereignty is to lie with the people

interventions.summary: Several members answer the Chair's question about whether the sitting should continue beyond five o'clock.
Patel characterises the House's preference as favouring adjournment at five rather than extending the sitting.
The Chair tests the House, finds the preference for five o'clock, and adjourns the Assembly until 11:00 AM on 17 December.
